source: Two different models have been proposed to explain how the endpoints of chromatin looped domains ('TADs') in eukaryotic chromosomes are determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the existence of two models in the scientific literature, supported by the subsequent description of these models and citations throughout the paper.

claim: In the loop-extrusion model, a cohesin complex extrudes a loop until it encounters a boundary element roadblock, generating a stem-loop.
source: In the first, a cohesin complex extrudes a loop until it encounters a boundary element roadblock, generating a stem-loop.

source: In this model, boundaries are functionally autonomous: they have an intrinsic ability to halt the movement of incoming cohesin complexes that is independent of the properties of neighboring boundaries.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of the loop-extrusion model as described in the literature.

claim: In the boundary-pairing model, loops are generated by boundary:boundary pairing.

source: Moreover, unlike the loop-extrusion model, pairing interactions can generate both stem-loops and circle-loops.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of the boundary-pairing model.

claim: The authors used MicroC to analyze how TADs are organized.
source: We have used a combination of MicroC to analyze how TADs are organized, and experimental manipulations of the even skipped TAD boundary, homie, to test the predictions of the 'loop-extrusion' and the 'boundary-pairing' models.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The authors experimentally manipulated the even skipped TAD boundary, homie, to test model predictions.
source: We have used a combination of MicroC to analyze how TADs are organized, and experimental manipulations of the even skipped TAD boundary, homie, to test the predictions of the 'loop-extrusion' and the 'boundary-pairing' models.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The findings are incompatible with the loop-extrusion model.

evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The endpoints of TADs in flies are determined by a mechanism in which boundary elements physically pair with their partners, either head-to-head or head-to-tail, with varying degrees of specificity.
source: Our findings are incompatible with the loop-extrusion model, and instead suggest that the endpoints of TADs in flies are determined by a mechanism in which boundary elements physically pair with their partners, either head-to-head or head-to-tail, with varying degrees of specificity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The mechanism for TAD formation in flies is unlikely to require loop extrusion.
source: Although our experiments do not address how partners find each other, the mechanism is unlikely to require loop extrusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Chromosomes of multicellular animals have a regular and inheritable physical organization.
source: The chromosomes of multicellular animals have a regular and inheritable physical organization.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to historical and contemporary research.

claim: Chromosome organization was first recognized in studies on lampbrush chromosomes in amphibian oocytes and polytene chromosomes of insects.
source: This was first recognized in studies on the lampbrush chromosomes in amphibian oocytes and the polytene chromosomes of insects (Callan, 1963; Nora et al., 2020; Zhimulev and Belyaeva, 1991; Zhimulev et al., 1983).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations to the original research.

claim: The architectural features inferred from analysis of lampbrush and polytene chromosomes are present in chromosomes throughout much of the animal kingdom.
source: Subsequent research has shown that the architectural features inferred from analysis of lampbrush and polytene chromosomes are present in chromosomes throughout much of the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by subsequent research in the field.

claim: The key organizational principle of chromosomes is the subdivision of the chromatin fiber into a series of independent looped domains, commonly called 'TADs'.
source: The key organizational principle is the subdivision of the chromatin fiber into a series of independent looped domains, commonly called 'TADs' (Cavalheiro et al., 2021; Chetverina et al., 2017; Jerković et al., 2020; Matthews and White, 2019; Rowley and Corces, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The arrangement of TADs along a given chromosome tend to be invariant and are largely independent of the cell type or developmental stage, with important exceptions.
source: With important exceptions, the arrangement of TADs along a given chromosome tend to be invariant and are largely independent of the cell type or developmental stage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TAD organization.

claim: TADs are separated from each other by special elements called boundaries or insulators.
source: TADs are separated from each other by special elements called boundaries or insulators.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromosome organization.

claim: Boundary elements have been found in many different species but have been most fully characterized in Drosophila.
source: While these elements have been found in many different species, they have been most fully characterized in Drosophila (Cavalheiro et al., 2021; Chetverina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Fly boundaries span DNA sequences of 150 bp to 1.5 kb in length.
source: Fly boundaries span DNA sequences of 150 bp to 1.5 kb in length and contain one or more nucleosome-free nuclease-hypersensitive regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physical characteristics of fly boundaries.

claim: Fly boundaries contain one or more nucleosome-free nuclease-hypersensitive regions.
source: Fly boundaries span DNA sequences of 150 bp to 1.5 kb in length and contain one or more nucleosome-free nuclease-hypersensitive regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural features of fly boundaries.

claim: Nuclease-hypersensitive regions in fly boundaries are targets for a large collection of DNA binding proteins that have been implicated in boundary function.
source: These nuclease-hypersensitive regions are targets for a large collection of DNA binding proteins that have been implicated in boundary function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular composition of boundaries.

claim: Some fly boundary factors are widely conserved (CTCF, BEN family proteins, GAF).
source: Some of the fly boundary factors are widely conserved (CTCF, BEN family proteins, GAF), while others appear to be restricted to insect linages (Su(Hw), Pita, Zw5, Zipic, Mod(mdg4), BEAF; Heger et al., 2013; Heger and Wiehe, 2014; Schoborg and Labrador, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary conservation of boundary proteins, supported by citations.

claim: Some fly boundary factors appear to be restricted to insect lineages (Su(Hw), Pita, Zw5, Zipic, Mod(mdg4), BEAF).
source: Some of the fly boundary factors are widely conserved (CTCF, BEN family proteins, GAF), while others appear to be restricted to insect linages (Su(Hw), Pita, Zw5, Zipic, Mod(mdg4), BEAF; Heger et al., 2013; Heger and Wiehe, 2014; Schoborg and Labrador, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary distribution of boundary proteins, supported by citations.

claim: Boundary elements in flies are responsible for organizing the chromatin fiber.
source: Boundary elements in flies are not only responsible for organizing the chromatin fiber, they also have genetic activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about boundary function.

claim: Boundary elements in flies have genetic activities.
source: Boundary elements in flies are not only responsible for organizing the chromatin fiber, they also have genetic activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about boundary function.

claim: When interposed between enhancers or silencers and target promoters, boundary elements block regulatory interactions.
source: When interposed between enhancers or silencers and target promoters, boundary elements block regulatory interactions (Bell et al., 2001; Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about boundary function, supported by citations.

claim: The insulating activity of boundary elements provides a mechanism for delimiting units of independent gene activity.
source: This insulating activity provides a mechanism for delimiting units of independent gene activity: genes located between a pair of compatible boundaries are subject to regulatory interactions with enhancers/silencers present in the same chromosomal interval, while they are insulated from the effects of enhancers/silencers located beyond either boundary in adjacent neighborhoods.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequence of boundary insulating activity.

claim: Genetic studies suggest that the insulating activity of boundary elements is a consequence of subdividing the chromosome into a series of topologically independent domains.
source: Genetic studies suggest that the insulating activity of boundary elements is a consequence of subdividing the chromosome into a series of topologically independent domains (Cai and Shen, 2001; Gohl et al., 2011; Muravyova et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Organizing the chromatin fiber into looped domains enhances contacts between sequences within the loop, while it suppresses contacts with sequences outside of the loop.
source: Organizing the chromatin fiber into looped domains enhances contacts between sequences within the loop, while it suppresses contacts with sequences outside of the loop.
evidence: This is an inference about the physical consequences of loop formation.

claim: In mammals, a loop-extrusion model has been proposed to generate chromosomal loops and determine the endpoints of those loops.
source: In mammals, a novel loop-extrusion model has been proposed to not only generate chromosomal loops but also determine the endpoints of those loops (Alipour and Marko, 2012; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2015; Nuebler et al., 2018; Sanborn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the loop-extrusion model in mammals, supported by citations.

claim: In the loop-extrusion model, a cohesin complex initiates loop formation at a loading site within the 'loop-to-be' and then extrudes a chromatin loop until it bumps into CTCF-dependent roadblocks.
source: In this model, a cohesin complex initiates loop formation at a loading site within the 'loop-to-be' and then extrudes a chromatin loop until it bumps into CTCF-dependent roadblocks, one on each side of the extruding loop.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the loop-extrusion model.

claim: In the loop-extrusion model, the location of roadblocks combined with the processive action of the cohesin complex determines the endpoints of each TAD.
source: The location of these roadblocks combined with the processive action of the cohesin complex determines the endpoints of each TAD (Davidson and Peters, 2021; Ghosh and Meyer, 2021; Mirny and Dekker, 2022; Perea-Resa et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the loop-extrusion model, supported by citations.

claim: A key assumption of the loop-extrusion model is that mammalian boundaries are fully autonomous.
source: A key assumption of the loop-extrusion model is that mammalian boundaries are fully autonomous: they are roadblocks, and their physical presence in and of itself is sufficient to define the loop endpoint, independent of the functional properties of neighboring boundaries.
evidence: This describes a fundamental assumption of the loop-extrusion model.

claim: In a variant of the loop-extrusion model, the relative orientation of the paired CTCF roadblocks is important for halting cohesin-mediated extrusion.
source: In a more specific variant of this model, the relative orientation of the paired CTCF roadblocks is also important—in order to halt cohesin-mediated extrusion, the CTCF sites on each side of the loop must have a convergent orientation.
evidence: This describes a specific variant of the loop-extrusion model.

claim: In the orientation-dependent variant of the loop-extrusion model, CTCF roadblocks can block an oncoming cohesin complex in only one direction.
source: In this model, the CTCF roadblocks are able to block an oncoming cohesin complex in only one direction; however, their intrinsic blocking activity is independent of the orientation of other CTCF sites in their neighborhood.
evidence: This describes a feature of the orientation-dependent loop-extrusion model.

claim: The evidence regarding TAD formation and function in flies is seemingly inconsistent with the loop-extrusion mechanism.
source: While this loop-extrusion mechanism is widely thought to be operative in mammals, the evidence regarding TAD formation and function in flies is seemingly inconsistent with this mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of evidence in the field.

claim: Genetics studies have shown that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous.
source: Genetics studies have shown that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous and that their activities in both loop formation and gene regulation depend upon their ability to engage in direct physical interactions with other boundaries (Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: The activities of fly boundaries in both loop formation and gene regulation depend upon their ability to engage in direct physical interactions with other boundaries.
source: Genetics studies have shown that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous and that their activities in both loop formation and gene regulation depend upon their ability to engage in direct physical interactions with other boundaries (Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: The gypsy transposon su(Hw) boundary can mediate regulatory interactions between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more.
source: That fly boundaries might function by physical pairing was first suggested by studies which showed that the gypsy transposon su(Hw) boundary and the bithorax complex (BX-C) Mcp boundary can mediate regulatory interactions (enhancer/silencer: reporter) between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more (Muller et al., 1999; Sigrist and Pirrotta, 1997; Vazquez et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The bithorax complex (BX-C) Mcp boundary can mediate regulatory interactions between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more.
source: That fly boundaries might function by physical pairing was first suggested by studies which showed that the gypsy transposon su(Hw) boundary and the bithorax complex (BX-C) Mcp boundary can mediate regulatory interactions (enhancer/silencer: reporter) between transgenes inserted at sites separated by 15–32 Mb or more (Muller et al., 1999; Sigrist and Pirrotta, 1997; Vazquez et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Distant transgenes containing the same boundary co-localize in vivo and remain in contact for extended periods of time.
source: Consistent with direct physical interactions, these distant transgenes co-localize in vivo, and in living tissue remain in contact for extended periods of time (Chen et al., 2018; Li et al., 2011; Vazquez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Parameters that govern pairing interactions have been defined in insulator bypass and boundary competition transgene assays.
source: Some of the parameters that govern pairing interactions have been defined in two different transgene assays, insulator bypass and boundary competition.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description and citations to these assays.

claim: In the bypass assay, when a single boundary is introduced between enhancers and the closest reporter, the enhancers are unable to activate either reporter.
source: In one version of the bypass assay, a set of enhancers are placed upstream of two different reporters (Cai and Shen, 2001; Kyrchanova et al., 2008a; Muravyova et al., 2001). When a single boundary is introduced between the enhancers and the closest reporter, the enhancers are unable to activate either reporter.
evidence: This describes the results of the bypass assay, supported by citations.

claim: In the bypass assay, if the same boundary is placed downstream of the closest reporter, bypass is observed.
source: However, if the same boundary is placed downstream of the closest reporter, bypass is observed. In this case the closest reporter, which is bracketed by the two boundaries, is still insulated from the enhancers; however, the downstream reporter is activated (Muravyova et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the results of the bypass assay, supported by a citation.

claim: Bypass activity is, in most cases, orientation-dependent.
source: Kyrchanova et al., 2008a showed that bypass activity is, in most cases, orientation-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: When the same boundary is placed in the upstream and downstream position, they typically need to be introduced in the opposite orientation for bypass to occur.
source: When the same boundary is placed in the upstream and downstream position, they typically need to be introduced in the opposite orientation.
evidence: This describes the orientation dependence of bypass activity.

claim: Self-pairing of boundaries is head-to-head, and this configuration generates a stem-loop topology.
source: The reason for this is that self-pairing is head-to-head, and this configuration generates a stem-loop topology, bringing the upstream enhancers into close proximity to the downstream reporter.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of bypass based on the orientation dependence.

claim: When two boundaries are introduced in the same orientation, the enhancers do not activate the downstream reporter because a circle-loop rather than a stem-loop is formed.
source: When the two boundaries are introduced in the same orientation, the enhancers do not activate the downstream reporter because a circle-loop rather than a stem-loop is formed (Chetverina et al., 2017; Kyrchanova et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Head-to-head pairing is a common feature of self-pairing interactions between fly boundaries.
source: Head-to-head pairing seems to be a common feature of self-pairing interactions between fly boundaries and was observed for scs, scs', iA2 and wari (Kyrchanova et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work on multiple boundaries.

claim: A preference for head-to-head interactions is observed for heterologous pairing interactions between different boundaries in the Abdominal-B (Abd-B) region of the BX-C.
source: A preference for head-to-head interactions is also observed for heterologous pairing interactions between different boundaries in the Abdominal-B (Abd-B) region of the BX-C (Kyrchanova et al., 2011; Kyrchanova et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The BX-C Fab-7 boundary pairs with itself and with its neighbor Fab-8 in both orientations.
source: There are some exceptions. The BX-C Fab-7 boundary pairs with itself and with its neighbor Fab-8 in both orientations (Kyrchanova et al., 2011; Kyrchanova et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work showing an exception to the head-to-head pairing rule.

claim: When multimerized dCTCF or Zw5 binding sites are placed both upstream and downstream of the closest reporter, bypass is observed.
source: For example, when multimerized dCTCF or Zw5 binding sites are placed both upstream and downstream of the closest reporter, bypass is observed.
evidence: This describes experimental results showing partner specificity.

claim: There is no bypass when multimerized dCTCF sites are tested with multimerized Zw5 sites.
source: However, there is no bypass when multimerized dCTCF sites are tested with multimerized Zw5 sites (Kyrchanova et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work showing partner specificity.

claim: Similar partner specificity results have been reported for the Zipic and Pita factors.
source: Similar results have been reported for the Zipic and Pita factors (Zolotarev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Boundary:boundary pairing preferences are observed in competition assays.
source: Boundary:boundary pairing preferences are also observed in competition assays in which different boundaries are introduced into the same transgene (Gohl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: In competition assays, the insulating activity of a boundary in the blocking position can be compromised or lost if a heterologous boundary upstream of the enhancer is a better match for the boundary downstream of the reporter.
source: In these assays, the insulating activity of a boundary in the blocking position (between an enhancer and a reporter that is flanked by a 3' boundary) is challenged by placing a heterologous boundary upstream of the enhancer. If the boundary upstream of the enhancer is a better match for the boundary located downstream of the reporter, then the insulating activity of the boundary in the blocking position can be compromised or lost altogether.
evidence: This describes the results of competition assays, supported by the citation.

claim: Fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous—their activities depend upon their ability to physically interact with other boundaries.
source: These and other experiments argue that fly boundaries are functionally non-autonomous—that is, their activities depend upon their ability to physically interact with other boundaries.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited experimental evidence.

claim: The two models differ in the possible topologies of the chromatin loops that form TADs.
source: However, the differences between the two models are not limited to the mechanisms for determining the endpoints of TADs. The models also differ in the possible topologies of the chromatin loops that form TADs.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical differences between the models.

claim: Only two loop topologies can be generated by the cohesin-extrusion mechanism: a stem-loop and an unanchored loop.
source: Only two loop topologies can be generated by the cohesin-extrusion mechanism. One is a stem-loop while the other is an unanchored loop.
evidence: This is a theoretical constraint of the loop-extrusion model.

claim: In the loop-extrusion model, the chromatin fiber would be organized into a series of stem-loops separated by unanchored loops.
source: Depending upon the location of the roadblocks that halt cohesin extrusion and the cohesin loading sites, the chromatin fiber would be organized into a series of stem-loops. These stem-loops will be separated from each other by unanchored loops (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes a predicted organization pattern in the loop-extrusion model, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: If the relevant roadblocks are very closely juxtaposed in the loop-extrusion model, the unanchored connecting loops will disappear and be replaced by a series of stem-loops that point in opposite orientations.
source: If the relevant roadblocks are very closely juxtaposed, then the unanchored connecting loops will disappear and be replaced by a series of stem-loops that point in opposite orientations, as illustrated in Figure 1C.
evidence: This describes an alternative organization pattern in the loop-extrusion model, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Stem-loops are possible in the boundary-pairing model and will be formed when two heterologous boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail in cis.
source: Stem-loops are also possible in the boundary-pairing model, and they will be formed when two heterologous boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail in cis (see Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes a possible organization pattern in the boundary-pairing model, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: In the boundary-pairing model, stem-loops could be separated from each other by unanchored loops.
source: Like loop-extrusion, the stem-loops could be separated from each other by unanchored loops (Figure 1E).
evidence: This describes a possible organization pattern in the boundary-pairing model, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: If boundaries in the neighborhood pair with each other head-to-tail in the boundary-pairing model, a series of connected stem-loops pointing in opposite orientations will be generated.
source: If the boundaries in the neighborhood pair with each other head-to-tail, a series of connected stem-loops pointing in opposite orientations will be generated.
evidence: This describes a possible organization pattern in the boundary-pairing model.

claim: In the boundary-pairing model with head-to-tail pairing, the main axis of the chromosome would be a series of paired boundaries.
source: In this case, the main axis of the chromosome would be a series of paired boundaries (Figure 1F).
evidence: This describes the predicted chromosome structure in the boundary-pairing model, illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: If neighboring boundaries pair with each other head-to-head in the boundary-pairing model, a circle-loop structure will be generated.
source: If the neighboring boundaries pair with each other head-to-head instead of head-to-tail, a circle-loop structure will be generated (Figure 1G).
evidence: This describes a possible organization pattern in the boundary-pairing model, illustrated in Figure 1G.

claim: In the boundary-pairing model, circle-loops could be connected by unanchored loops.
source: Like stem-loops, the circle-loops could be connected by unanchored loops (Figure 1H).
evidence: This describes a possible organization pattern in the boundary-pairing model, illustrated in Figure 1H.

claim: If boundaries pair with both neighbors head-to-head in the boundary-pairing model, this will generate a series of linked circle-loops oriented in the same direction.
source: Alternatively, if boundaries pair with both neighbors head-to-head, this will generate a series of linked circle-loops oriented in (more or less) the same direction (see Figure 1I).
evidence: This describes a possible organization pattern in the boundary-pairing model, illustrated in Figure 1I.

claim: The eve locus is flanked by homie and nhomie boundaries.
source: homie together with nhomie flank the 16 kb eve locus, and these two elements share many of the properties of other fly boundaries (Fujioka et al., 2013; Fujioka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the eve locus, supported by citations.

claim: homie and nhomie share many of the properties of other fly boundaries.
source: homie together with nhomie flank the 16 kb eve locus, and these two elements share many of the properties of other fly boundaries (Fujioka et al., 2013; Fujioka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work characterizing these boundaries.

claim: nhomie and homie can mediate long-distance regulatory interactions.
source: Like the gypsy and Mcp boundaries, nhomie and homie can mediate long-distance regulatory interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description and citations.

claim: A lacZ reporter transgene containing homie inserted on one homolog can be activated by an eve enhancer in a homie-containing transgene inserted on the other homolog, over a distance of 2 Mb.
source: For example, a lacZ reporter transgene containing homie (or nhomie) inserted on one homolog can be activated by an eve enhancer in a homie- (or nhomie-) containing transgene inserted on the other homolog, over a distance of 2 Mb (Fujioka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Long-distance activation is observed in heterologous combinations of nhomie and homie, but not in combinations with phage lambda DNA.
source: Long-distance activation is also observed in heterologous combinations of nhomie and homie, but not in combinations with phage lambda DNA.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Fujioka et al., 2016.

claim: Regulatory interactions are observed when a homie- or nhomie-containing reporter is inserted at an attP landing site in the hebe gene, 142 kb upstream of the eve locus.
source: Similarly, regulatory interactions are observed when a homie- or nhomie-containing reporter is inserted at an attP landing site in the hebe gene, 142 kb upstream of the eve locus (Chen et al., 2018; Fujioka et al., 2016; Fujioka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: When a homie- or nhomie-containing reporter is inserted at the hebe attP site, the eve enhancers drive reporter expression during development in a pattern that mimics the stage- and tissue-specific expression of the endogenous eve gene.
source: In this case, the eve enhancers drive reporter expression during development in a pattern that mimics the stage- and tissue-specific expression of the endogenous eve gene.
evidence: This describes the experimental results from the cited studies.

claim: For homie, activation of a reporter depends on the orientation of the boundary relative to the reporter in the transgene.
source: Activation also depends upon the orientation of the boundary (5'→3') relative to the reporter in the transgene. For homie, the reporter must be located 'upstream' of the boundary (5'→3'), just like the eve enhancers (and eve gene) are 'upstream' of endogenous homie (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the orientation dependence of homie-mediated activation, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Little or no activation is observed when the relative orientation of homie and the reporter is reversed.
source: Little or no activation is observed when the relative orientation is reversed, so that the reporter is located 'downstream' of homie.
evidence: This describes the orientation dependence of homie-mediated activation.

claim: For nhomie, the reporter must be located 'downstream' to be activated by the eve enhancers.
source: For nhomie, the reporter must be located 'downstream', in the same relative position as that in which the eve enhancers and eve gene are located with respect to endogenous nhomie (5'→3': Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the orientation dependence of nhomie-mediated activation, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The eve TAD is defined by nhomie and homie boundaries.
source: As expected, the left and right boundaries of the eve TAD correspond to nhomie and homie, respectively, and sequences containing these two boundaries converge at the apex of the eve interaction triangle.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: All sequences within the eve TAD appear to come into contact with each other and define a high density of internal contact domain (HDIC).
source: All the sequences within the TAD appear to come into contact with each other and define a high density of internal contact domain (HDIC).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The eve TAD is a stem-loop, not a circle-loop.
source: As predicted by both the loop-extrusion and boundary-pairing models, the eve TAD is a stem-loop, not a circle-loop (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the MicroC data showing a volcano plume, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: A volcano plume is observed at the apex of the eve TAD because sequences flanking eve are brought into close proximity when homie and nhomie are linked to each other.
source: This is evident from the prominent 'volcano plume' at the apex of the eve TAD (volcano triangle). A volcano plume is observed because sequences flanking eve are brought into close proximity when homie and nhomie are linked to each other by either cohesin or by head-to-tail pairing (see Figure 1: see also Ke et al., 2024).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism generating the volcano plume, based on the MicroC data.

claim: The stem-loop structure of the eve TAD is required for boundary bypass, as it enables enhancers flanking the 'upstream' boundary to interact with reporters flanking the 'downstream' boundary.
source: This conclusion is supported by previous transgene studies. As first described in the boundary bypass experiments of Cai and Shen, 2001 and Muravyova et al., 2001, the formation of a stem-loop structure when two boundaries are linked together brings sequences immediately beyond the linked boundaries into close proximity with each other. In this assay, a stem-loop structure is required, as it enables enhancers flanking the 'upstream' boundary to interact with reporters flanking the 'downstream' boundary (Kyrchanova et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: A circle-loop configuration does not bring the neighbors to either side of eve into close proximity.
source: In contrast, a circle-loop configuration does not bring the neighbors to either side of eve into close proximity.
evidence: This is an inference about the topological consequences of circle-loop formation.

claim: One feature of the eve TAD is inconsistent with the loop-extrusion model: there are no vertical stripes or 45° stripes that would be expected from loop extrusion intermediates.
source: While a stem-loop is the topology expected for the eve TAD in both models, one feature of the TAD is inconsistent with the loop-extrusion model. According to this model, loops (TADs) are generated by a cohesin complex that forms a small bubble at a loading site somewhere in the TAD-to-be and then extrudes both strands of the growing loop at an equal rate until it bumps into the boundary roadblocks (Davidson and Peters, 2021; Ghosh and Meyer, 2021; Mirny and Dekker, 2022; Perea-Resa et al., 2021). If the loading site were located in the middle of the TAD-to-be, and the extrusion intermediates in a population of nuclei were captured by crosslinking, one should observe a crosslink-generated stripe that begins at the loading site and extends perpendicular to the chromosomal DNA until it reaches the apex that links the two TAD boundaries with imaginary lines of 45° (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). This is the pattern that would be generated by a 'broken zipper' when it transiently links the zipper teeth equidistant from the initial 'loading site' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). If the loading site is off center to the left, the crosslinking of the passing cohesin complex in a population of nuclei will generate a perpendicular stripe until cohesin come to a halt when it encounters the roadblock on the left (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C). Assuming that the complex continues to extrude the right strand, it will then generate a stripe at a 45° angle that extends to the apex of the TAD. If the loading site corresponds to one of the CTCF roadblocks or is located close to the roadblock, the cohesin complex will generate a 45° stripe that comes to a halt at the apex of the triangle when it encounters the neighboring CTCF roadblock (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E). If there are multiple loading sites within the TAD, there should be a series of perpendicular stripes that generate and sequentially reinforce the stripe(s) at 45° (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F). However, in spite of the fact that NC14 fly embryos should provide by far the best prospect of actually capturing loop extrusion intermediates, there are no vertical stripes in the eve TAD, nor are there stripes at 45° that extend to the apex of the eve TAD. Nor do we observe a population of perpendicular stripes that convert into a series of reinforced 45° stripes. There is also no evidence of stripes that are initially tilted to the left or right of a 'loading site', as might be observed if the rate of extrusion were unequal on the two strands, and then subsequently convert to a 45° stripe as cohesin comes to a halt at the first boundary encountered.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the MicroC data and comparison to theoretical predictions illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

source: The second mechanism for generating LDC domains would be switching and/or combining pairing partners (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H–J).

claim: In the loop-extrusion model, a cohesin complex initiating loop extrusion in the eve TAD must break through the nhomie roadblock and come to a halt at the homie boundary at –142 kb to generate the eveMammoth (eveMa) TAD.
source: In the loop-extrusion model, a cohesin complex initiating loop extrusion in the eve TAD must break through the nhomie roadblock at the upstream end of the eve TAD. It must then make its way past the boundaries that separate eve from the attP site in the hebe gene, and come to a halt at the homie boundary associated with the lacZ reporter. This would generate a novel TAD, eveMammoth (eveMa), that extends from the eve homie all the way to the homie fragment at –142 kb, and encompasses both the reporter and the eve gene, including its enhancers (c.f., Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the predicted mechanism in the loop-extrusion model, illustrated in Figure 3D.

source: Of course, the eveMa TAD could also be generated by a cohesin complex that initiated in, for example, TF. However, in this case, the runaway cohesin complex would have to break through the intervening boundary roadblocks in both directions.
evidence: This describes an alternative scenario in the loop-extrusion model.

evidence: This is observed in the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

evidence: This is observed in the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

Our studies do not support a loop-extrusion mechanism and are inconsistent with this model on multiple levels.

evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The orientation of the physical interactions that bring distant enhancers into close proximity with their gene targets determines whether the enhancer will be able to activate its target gene.
source: Our experiments highlight an important constraint on long-distance regulatory interactions that are mediated not only by boundary elements like homie, nhomie, and the meta-loop boundaries in Figure 9, but also by the GAF-dependent (LBC) tethering and bypass elements (Batut et al., 2022; Kyrchanova et al., 2023; Kyrchanova et al., 2018; Kyrchanova et al., 2019a; Kyrchanova et al., 2019b; Levo et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Mohana et al., 2023), namely the orientation of the physical interactions that bring distant enhancers (or silencers) into close proximity with their gene targets. As we have shown here, the orientation of the physical interactions that bring distant sequences close together determines whether the enhancer will be able to activate its target gene.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on orientation-dependent reporter activation.

evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in flies and general principles of chromosome organization.
